WINGTIP VORTICES
The cause of wingtip vortices at the end of the wing is the difference in pressure below and above the wing, while it generates lift. Near the end of the wing, the air with higher pressure is deflected outwards in a circular motion, and towards the lower pressure on the upper surface inwards. Parallel to the end of the wing, the main flow is deflected upwards, creating vortices in the shape of a wingtip vortex, which continues downwards behind the wing.
We can imagine that the confined vortices on the wing continue into confined vortices at the end of the wing in a U-shape. Because these vortices at the end of the wing cannot be interrupted, they continue behind the wing.
In practice, this picture is much more complex, as the vortices at the end of the wing affect the rest of the wing surface. The influence towards the wing root gradually weakens, and we get vortices behind the entire wing as shown in the drawing.
At a certain distance behind the wing, all the vortices merge into two simple vortices, and the horizontal distance between them is slightly less than the wingspan. These two vortices are the result of a large number of vortices on the wing, which makes it easier to understand the flow behavior behind the wing.
DOWNWASH
If we observe the wing from behind during flight, we notice a system of circular vortices as shown in the drawing. The vortices behind the wing create a downwash, and outside the wing, an upwash. This flow is not related to the vortices on the wing but is a consequence of the vortices at the end of the wing. These vortices do not produce useful lift but change the direction of the main flow along the entire wing.
The main flow, which is far enough from the wing, does not feel the influence of the vortices, but near the wing, there is an influence that depends on the strength of the end vortices. Due to the different influence of the downwash along the wing, the aerodynamic angle of attack changes accordingly. In the drawings, we can see that the induced vortices are an integral part of the reaction directed backwards.
The larger the geometric angle of attack, the larger the lift coefficient. As the lift coefficient increases, the end vortices and their shape behind the wing also increase. This increases the influence on the change in the aerodynamic angle of attack and the increase in induced drag.
Infinitely long wings do not have end vortices, so they do not produce induced drag and do not affect the change in the angle of attack. However, in practice, all wings have a finite size, so the influence of induced vortices is present on all wings. Long, slender wings with properly shaped wingtips come very close to the ideal infinite wing.
ASPECT RATIO
The aspect ratio of a wing or similar surface is obtained by dividing the wingspan by the mean chord. For composite or elliptical shapes, where the area is known, the aspect ratio can be calculated using the equation:
Acrobatic motor models have a small aspect ratio, while glider models, due to slow flight, need a high aspect ratio to reduce induced drag, reaching a value of up to 35.
INDUCED DRAG COEFFICIENT
The equation determines how large the effect of the aspect ratio is, which gives the size of the induced drag on the wing:
The correction factor is always slightly higher than 1 for a well-designed wing shape. The equation shows that doubling the aspect ratio reduces induced drag by half. The sinking speed of the model depends on the maximum value of the Cl1.5/Cd ratio. The highest drag coefficient is achieved at low speed because the induced drag increases significantly.
For example, we can see that increasing the aspect ratio from 7.5 to 15 raises the performance factor from 16:1 to 26:1. For this reason, high-performance gliders have a high aspect ratio.
A low sinking speed is very important for longer gliding time and better exploitation of thermals. With a high aspect ratio, the sinking speed is low, even if the wing loading is higher. The aspect ratio and wing loading can be coordinated to control the model's penetration. To minimize the sinking speed, we must use a high aspect ratio and low wing loading.
INFLUENCE OF ASPECT RATIO ON REYNOLDS NUMBER
Increasing the aspect ratio of the wing quickly leads to the problem of low Reynolds numbers. A high aspect ratio gives a small wing chord, so the wing flies in a region of low Reynolds numbers, which makes it difficult to achieve efficient flight. We must pay a lot of attention to this problem and choose an airfoil that has a very low critical Reynolds number.
INFLUENCE OF ASPECT RATIO ON SENSITIVITY
A very slender wing is naturally very sensitive to lift and drop in gusts of wind. This effect is very pronounced if we use an airfoil with a very low critical Reynolds number, which is very thin and therefore very sensitive to changes in the angle of attack and the behavior of the separation bubble on the upper surface of the wing. The lift coefficient value relative to the angle of attack is different for different aspect ratios.
The drawing shows the slope of the lift coefficient curve for three different aspect ratios. For a higher aspect ratio, the slope of the lift curve is greater than for a lower aspect ratio. To achieve the same lift coefficient, a wing with a low aspect ratio and a larger downwash behind the wing must have a larger geometric angle of attack. The aspect ratio at achieving a lift coefficient of 0 no longer has an influence on the angle of attack.

Thinner airfoils with a low critical Reynolds number have a slope value of the lift curve greater than 0.11 per degree, but with a higher aspect ratio, they become sensitive to changes in the angle of attack. The bending of the wing affects the change in stability and balance, and improperly made commands for controlling ailerons can block or cause flutter.
For wings with a high aspect ratio, it is very important that the hinges are mounted exactly in the middle, and the gap between the wing and the aileron is well sealed. To avoid blocking the commands, we mount the servomotors in the wings with the shortest possible connections to the ailerons.
INFLUENCE OF ASPECT RATIO ON ROLL
Models with a high aspect ratio are naturally slow in rolling. This is partly because the mass is distributed along the long wing and resists this. However, when the wing begins to tilt, it resists stopping this movement. In rolling, the half of the wing that rises has a smaller aerodynamic angle of attack, and the other half, which drops, has an increasing angle of attack. A force appears that resists rolling.
To ensure good rolling in aerobatics, we must overcome the braking effect with ailerons. In a turn, the outer half of the wing travels a longer distance than the inner half, so an even greater force appears that resists rolling. To overcome these braking forces, we must install larger ailerons. Glider models that do not use ailerons for steering should not have a high aspect ratio because the braking effect in a turn can weaken the rudder command too much.

A wing with a low aspect ratio is more efficient at a larger range of angles of attack, easier to trim, and less critical in a turn. Gusts of wind and other disturbances have less influence on such a wing. For its efficiency, it needs a sufficiently strong transverse flow to quickly stop the rolling. Surfaces with a high aspect ratio reach the critical angle of attack too quickly in such conditions. When building a vertical stabilizer, we often extend the surface along the back of the fuselage and thus effectively reduce the aspect ratio of the vertical stabilizer.

V zavoju se pojavi še ena težava, ker zunanja polovica krila leti hitreje kot notranja. Razlika sile vzgona na obeh polovicah krila nagiba model v vedno bolj nagnjen let. Z uporabo krilc lahko model vodimo pod točno določenim nagibom.
MAJHNA VITKOST KRILA
Krilo z majhno vitkostjo je bolj učinkovito pri večjem razponu vpadnih kotov, lažje za trimanje in manj kritično v zavoju. Sunki vetra in ostale motnje imajo na takšno krilo manjši vpliv. The Whole Truth About Antibiotics: When It’s Better to Refrain

Penicillin. Cephalosporins. Macrolides. Tetracyclines. Aminoglycosides.

To control pathogenic microorganisms from the mid-20th century, antibiotics were used, which can inhibit their survival. These substances can be obtained from mixtures of natural ingredients, as well as from living organisms.

Antibiotics can destroy bacteria, fungi, and other infectious cells. However, they are not effective against common infections such as the flu and ARF. Antibiotics destroy bacteria, prevent their regeneration, disrupt bioprocesses occurring within them, and negatively affect the cell membrane. This significantly hinders the development process and the very existence of the bacteria.

How Antibiotics Work

The action of antibiotics is characterized by:

- Selectivity.
High selectivity is generally desirable, as it allows for a reduction in the level of adverse effects of the drug on the body.
- Spectrum of action.
This determines the degree to which the antibiotic affects one or another type of bacteria. The wider the spectrum, the less harm the treatment causes to the overall state of the body. It should be known that it is the unjustified use of antibiotics that has led to the development of bacteria such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Bacteria adapt and eventually become resistant to the drug. The phrase "What doesn't kill us makes us stronger" is relevant here. Use antibiotics correctly and be careful with dosage and duration of treatment.

What Antibacterial Drugs Are Available?

Antibiotics are divided into groups. Considering the chemical structure of the drugs themselves, these groups include cephalosporins, penicillins, macrolides, tetracyclines, and aminoglycosides.

There are antibiotics such as levomycetin, levorin, and nystatin. These are no longer used in medicine because they do not show the results for which they should be used. Levomycetin, it turns out, causes more harm than good.

- Penicillins. Highly selective and effective. The Penicillium mold provided pharmacologists with antibiotics of this group. The preparations were very effective in combating bacterial development until microorganisms adapted to the new, extremely unfavorable conditions caused by the drugs. Now, penicillin is not effective, but later, highly effective semi-synthetic drugs were developed. We have long known a wide range of antibiotics: ampicillin, amoxicillin (amoxiclav), carbenicillin.
- Cephalosporins. Included in the beta-lactam group. They differ in their ability to suppress bacteria that are not sensitive to penicillins. These antibiotics are divided into 3 generations: - the first generation is a drug that is easily tolerated by the human body. They are used for infectious diseases of the respiratory, urinary, and genital systems. These include cefalotin, cefazolin, cefalexin. - the second generation are drugs that are suitable for the treatment of the respiratory tract, stomach, and intestines. It should be noted that these drugs negatively affect the work of the gastrointestinal tract. These include cefuroxime, cefamadol. - The third generation is a wide range of drugs. They remain in the body for a long time and resist bacteria that are resistant to first-generation drugs. One of the side effects is a negative effect on the intestinal microflora. Third-generation antibiotics include ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, cefoperazone.
- Macrolides. They affect protein synthesis and are used to treat diseases such as chlamydia and atypical pneumonia. Macrolides do not harm human health. The drugs are very effective due to their ability to penetrate cells and destroy organisms that do not have membranes. These include the long-established erythromycin, as well as roxithromycin and azithromycin.
- Tetracyclines. They are used for severe infections. Like macrolides, they penetrate the cell and create a barrier to protein synthesis, but they differ in their broad spectrum of action. This often leads to disruption of biochemical processes that constantly occur in the human body. Tetracyclines should not be used in children under 14 years of age, and of course, not in pregnant women (as this can cause various complications and fetal deformities). These drugs include doxycycline and tetracycline.
- Aminoglycosides. Their use is necessary if there is an infection in the blood, such as tuberculosis. Treatment of the disease is serious and difficult. Aminoglycosides can cope with the problem, but their high toxicity is harmful to the liver, kidneys, and hearing. These include streptomycin and gentamicin.
- Levomycetin inhibits the formation of proteins and prevents the reproduction of bacteria. Its major drawback is its spectrum of action: it is unreasonably broad and therefore causes a lot of harm to the body. (The drug has a harmful effect on the bone marrow).
- Antifungal antibiotics affect and destroy membranes. However, they are not effective enough and cannot affect the state of the organism to a significant extent. These include nystatin and levorin.

In What Cases Is It Better to Refrain from Antibiotics?

The body and health of each individual are unique. This is something that doctors must take into account when prescribing medication. They consider the chemical properties, spectrum of action, and degree of toxicity. In some cases, taking antibiotics is dangerous:

- During pregnancy, the body is particularly susceptible to chemicals. However, the danger threatens not only the woman: the drugs negatively affect the fetus, especially in the first three months of its development. The likelihood of congenital malformations and anomalies increases, although, if necessary, penicillins and macrolides are used. These are the least toxic.
- Breastfeeding mothers should refrain from breastfeeding for 2 to 3 weeks if they need to take antibiotics. This will prevent chemicals from entering the child's body through milk.
- A baby's body is very sensitive to antibiotics: biochemical processes, the production of necessary proteins, etc., change. Therefore, only drugs such as penicillins, macrolides, and cephalosporins can be used.
- People with impaired kidney or liver function can only take penicillins or cephalosporins. Chronic diseases such as hepatitis, pyelonephritis, and kidney failure can worsen and make the administration of strong antibiotics more difficult.
- There are antibiotics (such as penicillins and cephalosporins) that can cause allergic reactions. Every doctor must remember this when prescribing medication. To avoid side effects, it is necessary to:
- strictly follow the doctor's instructions for dosage;
- combine drugs only with the permission of the attending physician;
- carefully monitor the expiration date of the drug;
- take probiotics to avoid dysbiosis;
- see a doctor if you notice any side effects.

Several open-source LLMs were released over the past couple of years. The most relevant models for less-resourced languages are multi-lingual models, which were trained on many languages; however, English still represents the majority of their training data. The best performing open-source multi-lingual models that include Slovene are EuroLLM~\cite{euro_llm}, Gemma 2~\cite{gemma2}, Gemma 3~\cite{gemma3}, DeepSeek~\cite{deepseek}, Qwen~\cite{qwen3}, Llama 4~\cite{llama4}, Mistral~\cite{mistral}, and Apertus~\cite{apertus}. The models such as DeepSeek, Llama 4, and the largest versions of Mistral and Qwen are often infeasible to run on-premises due to a large number of parameters that require a significant amount of GPU vRAM (usually more than 640 GB). Smaller versions of Mistral and Qwen, on the other hand, perform significantly worse on Slovene and are beaten by other models of similar size. Even though EuroLLM and Apertus were developed in the EU and are targeting European languages, they perform worse than Gemma on low-resource languages such as Slovene.

Gemma is an open-source model family released by Google. Their latest model, Gemma 3, is multi-modal (it can process images as well) and is the best-performing medium-sized open-source model for less-resourced languages. However, the creators do not reveal their training data and exact training procedure. One interesting detail they revealed is that they used UniMax~\cite{unimax} sampling strategy to handle the imbalance in the multi-lingual data representation. This approach clearly helped with the model's performance on less-resourced languages such as Slovene. Despite performing better than other multi-lingual models, Gemma 3 still lacks the knowledge of the specifics of less-resourced languages and cultures, and still benefits from language adaptation, as shown by our GaMS 3 model~\cite{gams3} for Slovene (part of this proposal).

Besides multi-lingual models, open sovereign models are also developed. One of the first such decoder-type models was the GPT-SW3~\cite{gpt-sw3} family for Swedish. This family was trained from scratch on a combination of $320$~B Swedish, Norwegian, Danish, Icelandic, English, and programming code tokens, which is not possible for less-resourced languages. The first models that applied language transfer were Chinese LLaMa \cite{chinese_llama} and Open-Chinese-LLaMA \cite{open_chinese_llama} for Chinese, and Gervasio \cite{gervasio} for Portuguese. However, these models were adapted only in the SFT phase and therefore lack target cultural knowledge. Currently, there are many initiatives across Europe, Asia, and the Middle East to build language-specific models, many of which are supported by NVIDIA's Sovereign AI initiative. The most relevant Sovereign model for our objectives is Polish Bielik~\cite{bielik}. Bielik is based on the Mistral 7B v0.2 architecture and scaled up to 11 billion parameters. Its training pipeline consists of 4 stages: CPT on 1.1 trillion tokens, SFT, and two preference alignment stages - Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Even though the Polish team used fewer resources than most of the SOTA English-based models, their training data is significantly larger than available for most less-resourced languages and therefore this approach is not completely applicable to less-resourced languages.

Several LLMs were already developed for Slovene. Encoder-type and encoder-decoder-type models include CroSloEngual BERT~\cite{cse_bert}, SloBERTa~\cite{sloberta}, and SloT5~\cite{slot5}. The first decoder-type models adapted for Slovene were SlovenianGPT~\cite{slovenian_gpt}, GaMS-1B~\cite{GaMS}, and TinySLlama~\cite{tiny_sllama}. Due to their older architecture, shorter contexts, and limited training data, these models are less useful in practice compared to most current open models. However, they provide valuable insights into the Slovenian specialization. They show the benefits of training the model combined with languages similar to Slovene, such as Croatian (CroSloEngual BERT), and the impact of vocabulary modification and embedding transfer (GaMS-1B). Currently, the most relevant Slovene specialized decoder-type LLMs are Gemma 2 based GaMS models~\cite{gams_9b} with 9B and 27B parameters, Mistral NeMo based Zlatorog 12B~\cite{zlatorog} and Gemma 3 based GaMS3-12B~\cite{gams3}. The best performing model out of these is GaMS-27B-Instruct-Nemotron~\cite{gams_27b_nemotron}. Compared to GaMS3, other GaMS models and Zlatorog were trained on much less data (around 15B tokens) and on much shorter contexts (Zlatorog has the longest context window with 16k tokens), making them useless on longer texts. GaMS3, on the other hand was trained on around 140B tokens and supports the context window of 131k tokens. All these models still lack cultural adaptation, especially in the SFT stage. Moreover, neither of them was preference-tuned yet.

The majority of works related to data collection and curation for all training stages focus on English data. The most relevant among open-source datasets are NVIDIA's Nemotron pre-training and post-training datasets~\cite{nemotron_sft, nemotron_sft_v2, nemotron_cc}. Interesting datasets for the CPT stage are parallel corpora, such as DGT~\cite{dgt} from the European Comission, that enable explicit parallel alignment of the languages and therefore speed up the knowledge transfer between languages, which is essential for less-resourced languages. A relevant method for such alignment is Align aFter Pre-training (AFP)~\cite{align_after_pretrain}, which we slightly adapted and moved to the CPT stage when training the GaMS models. Due to the lack of data for less-resourced languages, web crawls represent significant portion of data for such languages. However, web crawls often contain low-quality data, which must either be discarded or enhanced. One such enhancement method is ReWire~\cite{rewire}, which boosts the educational value of web data. The most relevant sources of SFT and preference alignment data are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Chatbot arenas, such as LMSYS~\cite{lmsys}, that collect the real-world distribution of human prompts.
    \item Methods for synthetic data generation such as Self-Instruct~\cite{self_instruct}.
\end{enumerate}
We currently observe a lack of frameworks for cultural adaptation of existing English chat datasets.

Slovenians are a nation whose identity as a distinct group can be traced back to at least the 16th century, with its roots in the early medieval principality of Carantania.
On December 26th, Slovenians celebrate Independence and Unity Day, commemorating the official announcement of the results of the 1990 plebiscite on Slovenian independence, in which the majority of Slovenia's population voted in favor of establishing an independent and sovereign state for the Slovenian nation.
This holiday provides an opportunity to delve into the history of the Slovenes, especially given recent arguments, even within Slovenian historiography, that the Slovenes as a distinct identity group only emerged in the 19th century. However, the facts suggest otherwise.
1. Fact
The name "Slovene" or "Slav" is an ancient linguistic self-designation used by the people referred to in historiography as Proto-Slavs or Ancient Slavs, at least since the late ancient period, and possibly even earlier. The word "Slovene" or "Slav" originates from the verb "sloviti," which means "to speak." The opposite of the term "Slovene" is "German." This is a somewhat mocking term for a member of a people who are supposedly "dumb" or unable to speak.
2. Fact
The ancestors of today's Slovenes settled in the territory between the Danube and the Adriatic in the second half of the 6th century. In the 7th century, they established the first Slavic state, Carantania, whose core was located in present-day Carinthia, excluding the short-lived Samo's Tribal Union. From the 9th century onwards, the name "Carantanian" became an ethnic name for all the ancestors of the Slovenes who lived between the Danube and the Adriatic for several centuries.
3. Fact
Due to the later fragmentation of the Slovenes into different regions, the name "Carantanian" as a common ethnic name faded into obscurity. In the regions where, in addition to Slovene speakers, there were also large numbers of German, Hungarian, or Italian speakers, the name "Slovene" re-emerged (Carinthia, Styria, Prekmurje, Venetian Slovenia, etc.), except in Carniola, where the term "Carniola" became synonymous with "Slovene" because Slovene speakers predominated.
4. Fact
The name "Slovene" as a designation for a national and linguistic community first appeared in written sources with Primož Trubar (1508-1586), who called the language he wrote in the Slovene language and the readers he addressed in that language "Slovenes." Initially, Trubar included Croats in the community of people who spoke his Slovene language, along with Carniolans, Lower Carniolans, Carinthians, Styrians, Krajina Slovenes, Istrians, and Kajkavians, but he soon "excluded" them from this community and clearly distinguished between speakers of the Slovene language and the Croatian language.
5. Fact
Trubar used the term "windische sprach(e)" in German for the Slovene language and "crobatische sprach(e)" for the Croatian language. Trubar also included Kajkavians among the speakers of the Slovene language, because the Germans used the ethnic term "windisch" to refer to the Slavic population in the south of the Holy Roman Empire, including Kajkavians, until the 17th century, and also in the neighboring Kingdom of Hungary.

These are the words that the Slovenes spread around the world
6. Fact
Although Trubar included Kajkavians in his Slovene linguistic community (the Kajkavians themselves also used the self-designation "Slovene" at the time and only definitively adopted the name "Croat" in the 18th century), he emphasized that the Kajkavians were similar in customs to Hungarians and Croats and that they had some linguistic peculiarities, so he ethnically distinguished between "Windisch" (Slovenes, including Kajkavians) and "Oberwindisch" (Slovenes without Kajkavians) in German.
7. Fact
The true, narrower ethnic community to which Trubar belonged was therefore the Carniolans and Slovenes ("Carniola and Slovenes"), one nation using two names, or in German, "dies Creynerisch vnd Oberwindisch gutherzig Volck" (Slovene: this Carniolan and Slovene good-hearted people).

Why is Slovene a manly language?
8. Fact
In the 18th century, the century of the Slovene national revival, some individuals, such as the Carniolan Marko Pohlin, distinguished between Carniolans and Slovenes (i.e., between Carniolans and Slovene-speaking Carinthians and Styrians), but the belief in one nation – the Slovene nation – soon prevailed again. A similar situation existed among the Czechs, who were divided into Czechs in the narrower sense of the word and Moravians, but both formed the Czech nation, which speaks the Czech language.
9. Fact
In the first half of the 19th century, the Slovenes already formulated their first political demands (United Slovenia) and rejected the Illyrian movement and the idea of linguistic unification with the Serbo-Croatian-speaking population beyond the Kolpa River.
10. Fact
The Slovene aspiration for national self-determination was finally realized in June 1991, when an independent and sovereign Slovenia was proclaimed on the basis of the plebiscite decision of December 1990 (the plebiscite was held on December 23, and the official announcement of the results was on December 26).

Yang Hsin-Fu in kolegi ugotovili, da se črevesna celice imunskega sistema imenovane prirojeno limfnega 3 vrste celic (ILC3s), je manj verjetno, da se odzovejo na patogene bakterije, če nimajo beljakovino, imenovano ID2. ILC3s celice, ki manjkala ID2 protein, ni bilo mogoče pripraviti molekule, imenovan IL-22, ki nato stimulira druge celice črevesja, da dobimo protimikrobnih peptidov (A). Ti ojačevalci pomagajo varovati telo pred oportunistične okužbe. Omeniti je treba, da se zdi, so normalne bakterije bolj odporne na amperov.
Ko je skupina znanstvenikov iz mikrofloro miši pretrpeli s temi slabše ILC3s celic v povsem sterilnem črevesja drugi miši, so bili prejemniki zelo dovzetna za okužbe, ko so kasneje podlegel okužbe s patogenimi bakterijami. Miši z sterilno črevesju, ki je prejela mikrofloro živali z navadno ILC3s celic, ki se lahko borijo škodljive bakterije.
Kako imunske celice razlikovati med zdravimi in patogenih bakterij, da se ohrani zdravo mikrofloro, je še vedno neznan, čeprav lahko patogeni proizvajajo molekule, ki lahko imunske celice prepozna. Ugotovljeno je bilo, da po okužbi ILC3s celice proizvajajo veliko število antimikrobnih peptidov.
Dr. Yang-Xin Fu je poudaril, da je človeško telo in njegovo mikroflora razvil, da živijo v harmoniji, skozi milijone let. "Ti vzajemno koristni odnosi nam omogočajo, da pravilno prejeli vseh hranil iz naše hrane in, kot je prikazano v tej študiji, sposobnost omejiti okužbe s patogenimi bakterijami povzročajo," - Yang-Xin Fu je dejal.
